title: Commutes Sentence of Traie Tavares Kelly
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Traie Tavares Kelly as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted Traie Tavares Kelly’s federal sentence. The Justice Department lists Kelly’s District of South Carolina conviction for conspiring to distribute cocaine base and cocaine, with a 240-month prison term and 10 years of supervised release imposed on January 7, 2009. Its public listing does not give the replacement sentence or the reason for the commutation.
description_long: Donald Trump commuted Traie Tavares Kelly’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. The Justice Department’s commutation list identifies Kelly’s case in the District of South Carolina and describes the conviction as a conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and distribute at least 50 grams of cocaine base and at least 5 kilograms of cocaine. It lists the original sentence as 240 months in prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release, imposed on January 7, 2009. Those details show the sentence in place before Trump’s action, but the page does not state what prison term or supervision Trump substituted, whether Kelly was released immediately, or how much of the original sentence remained. A commutation changes punishment but leaves the conviction in force. The listed case details therefore provide context for the sentence Trump altered, while the clemency record leaves the practical extent of the reduction and the reason for Kelly’s selection unstated.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Traie Tavares Kelly
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Traie Tavares Kelly as part of a clemency list.

notes: The Justice Department list supports the offense, district, original 240-month sentence, and 10 years of supervised release. It does not give the amended terms or a rationale, and it supplies no evidence for the “Corrupt Pardons” characterization.
proposed_correction: Describe this as a commutation of a federal drug sentence. Do not characterize the action as corrupt without evidence of improper favoritism or an exchange; retain the missing amended sentence terms as unresolved.

title: Commutes Sentence of Ferrell Damon Scott
description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Ferrell Damon Scott as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: On January 19, 2021, Donald Trump commuted Ferrell Damon Scott’s federal sentence. The Justice Department lists a Southern District of Texas case involving marijuana-distribution offenses, an original life sentence, 10 years of supervised release, and a $10,000 fine imposed on April 2, 2009. The public listing does not specify the sentence Trump substituted or whether the other penalties changed.
description_long: Donald Trump commuted Ferrell Damon Scott’s federal sentence on January 19, 2021. The Justice Department’s list places Scott’s case in the Southern District of Texas and identifies a conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute more than 1,000 kilograms of marijuana, along with three counts of possessing more than 100 kilograms with intent to distribute. The original sentence, dated April 2, 2009, included life imprisonment, 10 years of supervised release, and a $10,000 fine. The life term makes the scale of the sentence reduction important, but the public clemency listing does not state the amended prison term or say whether the supervision and fine remained in effect. A commutation changes punishment without vacating the conviction. The record confirms a presidential sentence commutation in a serious drug case, but it gives no reason for Scott’s selection and no evidence of a private benefit or improper exchange. The amended clemency order is needed to establish the practical result of the action.

preserved_fields.title: Commutes Sentence of Ferrell Damon Scott
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump commuted the sentence of Ferrell Damon Scott as part of a clemency list.

notes: The Justice Department list supports the underlying offenses and original life sentence, supervised release, and fine. It omits the amended terms and gives no rationale or evidence for the “Corrupt Pardons” characterization.
proposed_correction: Describe this as a commutation of a federal marijuana sentence; do not imply corruption absent evidence of improper favoritism or exchange. Obtain the amended clemency terms before stating the sentence reduction.

title: Cambridge Analytica Tied to Trump Campaign Data Operations
description_short: Reports revealed Cambridge Analytica’s role in the Trump campaign and its use of Facebook data to influence voters.
description_medium: The March 17, 2017 entry concerns reports linking Cambridge Analytica to the Trump campaign’s data operations and its use of Facebook information to profile voters. The account raises questions about political targeting and privacy, but it does not identify the campaign contract, the data collection method, or how the resulting profiles were used in specific campaign decisions.

preserved_fields.title: Cambridge Analytica Tied to Trump Campaign Data Operations
preserved_fields.description_short: Reports revealed Cambridge Analytica’s role in the Trump campaign and its use of Facebook data to influence voters.

notes: The supplied Britannica link is about Cambridge, England, not Cambridge Analytica. The synopsis asserts a Trump campaign connection and use of Facebook data, but the packet provides no relevant reporting or details to substantiate those core claims.
proposed_correction: Replace the unrelated Britannica citation with reporting that documents Cambridge Analytica’s campaign role and Facebook-data practices before presenting the title and synopsis as established facts.

title: Michigan Supreme Court Keeps Trump on Primary Ballot
description_short: Michigan’s Supreme Court rejected an appeal seeking to disqualify Trump from the 2024 primary ballot.
description_medium: On December 27, 2023, Michigan’s Supreme Court rejected an appeal by Free Speech For People seeking to remove Donald Trump from the state’s 2024 presidential primary ballot. The challenge invoked Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment, which bars people who engaged in insurrection from holding office. The ruling left Trump on Michigan’s primary ballot.
description_long: Michigan’s Supreme Court rejected an appeal seeking to disqualify Donald Trump from the state’s 2024 presidential primary ballot on December 27, 2023. The appeal, brought by the advocacy group Free Speech For People, argued that Section 3 of the Fourteenth Amendment barred Trump from office because of his role in the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. The ruling left him on the Michigan ballot. The court noted that Colorado’s election laws differed from Michigan’s in a material way; Colorado’s high court had recently disqualified Trump from its primary ballot, though that order was delayed pending appeal. Michigan’s decision also reinforced a lower-court ruling that state election officials could not decide a presidential candidate’s eligibility under the state’s primary process and that Trump had not violated Michigan election law by filing. The decision resolved the state ballot challenge under Michigan’s election framework. It did not settle Section 3 questions nationwide or dictate the outcome of cases under other states’ laws.

preserved_fields.title: Michigan Supreme Court Keeps Trump on Primary Ballot
preserved_fields.description_short: Michigan’s Supreme Court rejected an appeal seeking to disqualify Trump from the 2024 primary ballot.

notes: The linked CNBC report supplies the challenger, constitutional basis, Michigan court’s reasoning about differing state election laws, and the ballot result; no material context remains missing for this event.

title: Immigration Courts Lose a Quarter of Judges After Trump Firings
description_short: NPR reported the immigration court system has about 25% fewer judges after widespread firings and resignations.
description_medium: NPR reported on February 23, 2026, that U.S. immigration courts had about one-quarter fewer permanent judges than a year earlier, after firings and resignations outweighed new hires. The number fell from 683 immigration judges and 43 assistant chief judges to 520 and 33. The report linked the staffing losses to mounting backlogs and strain on due process.
description_long: NPR’s February 23, 2026, analysis found that the immigration court system had about one-quarter fewer permanent judges than a year earlier, despite new hires. On February 4, 2025, the system had 683 immigration judges and 43 assistant chief judges across 75 courts; by the report’s publication, it had 520 and 33. The administration fired nearly 100 judges during 2025, and resignations added to the decline. Twelve courts had lost more than half their judges, while two had none. The Justice Department’s Executive Office for Immigration Review also lost more than 400 legal assistants, attorney advisers, and legal administrative specialists. NPR described mounting case backlogs, depleted staff morale, and pressure on due process in a system already handling thousands of cases. Former judges warned that the losses could undermine fairness and confidence; the Justice Department defended the staffing decisions as part of an effort to complete cases on time and protect public safety. The reported staffing figures establish a broad loss of adjudication capacity, though they do not by themselves show that any particular case was decided unfairly.

preserved_fields.title: Immigration Courts Lose a Quarter of Judges After Trump Firings
preserved_fields.description_short: NPR reported the immigration court system has about 25% fewer judges after widespread firings and resignations.

notes: The linked NPR report provides dated staffing totals, numbers of judges dismissed and support staff lost, court-level effects, and attributed assessments of backlogs and due process. The entry’s approximate one-quarter decline is supported.
